newsitem.title: USA: INS promises no mass deportations after April 1.
newsitem.headline: INS promises no mass deportations after April 1.

text.p: A sweeping new immigration law, parts of which go into effect on April 1, will not bring about any mass deportations of aliens, the U.S Immigration and Naturalisation Service said on Wednesday.

Contrary to persistent rumours in some immigrant communities, there is no benefit to aliens in marrying a U.S. citizen before the law kicks in, INS Deputy Commissioner Chris Sale told a news conference.
"The law does not (provide for), nor will we engage in, mass deportation," Sale said, adding: "The law does not mean that immigrants must file for a change in status or get married before April 1."

The law, signed last September, has sparked panic in some communities with large immigrant populations, creating lengthy lines outside marriage offices and a steep rise in requests for a change in immigrant status.

The purpose of the law is to tighten U.S. borders against illegal aliens by increasing the number of border patrol agents, improving technology and beefing up barriers along the U.S.-Mexican border. Deportation procedures will be streamlined and the number of aliens who are exempted from deportation will be capped.

Also starting on April 1, those foreigners who are not eligible to enter the United States will face "expedited removal" at ports of entry, according to Paul Virtue, an INS lawyer charged with implementing the new law.
In addition, the law cuts off federal food stamps and disability payments to legal immigrants, a provision that advocates for the poor challenged in a class-action lawsuit filed on Wednesday.

Public-interest law offices filed suit in federal district court in New York on behalf of about 100,000 legal immigrants in New York, Vermont and Connecticut, arguing that the law violates the Constitution's guarantee of equal protection.

The government has begun mailing out notices to hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants warning them they could lose disability benefits by August. Legal immigrants will also begin losing eligibility for Food Stamps starting in April.

One of those represented in the suit is Ekaterina Drubich, an 87-year-old Holocaust survivor who left the former Soviet Union in 1980. She is partially paralysed, has had a mastectomy and is too frail to travel on her own.
"I find it inconceivable that the same country that welcomed me as a refugee would allow me to go hungry and homeless," Drubich said in a statement.
